themes.theme: Information from providers for interpreting and checking outputs
themes.definition: Information, documentation and design features that providers must or should supply so that whoever deploys an AI tool can use it as intended, interpret its outputs and check its performance.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act makes the instructions for use the main channel: high-risk systems 'shall be accompanied by instructions for use' with concise, complete, correct and clear information (Art. 13(2)-(3)), including the accuracy level and metrics against which the system 'has been tested and validated' (Art. 13(3)(b)(ii), Art. 15(3)) and the technical measures that help deployers interpret outputs (Art. 13(3)(d)); the system itself must be transparent enough 'to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately' (Art. 13(1)) and be supplied so that overseers can stay aware of automation bias (Art. 14(4)(b)). Art. 9(5)(c) adds information and, 'where appropriate', training for deployers as a risk-reduction measure, and Recitals 65, 72 and 74 urge providers to communicate performance metrics 'in a clear and easily understandable way'. The instructions for use are also named as an input to the deployer's fundamental rights impact assessment (Recital 96; EU043). Outside the AI Act the same idea appears for EU institutions' own use: the European Parliament's 2020 guidelines say knowledge of a solution's inner workings 'must be available to both providers and users' before deployment, and the EDPS says technical and user documentation, 'including model cards', should let the controller carry out accuracy checks 'regularly'. The EDPB (EU074) treats a developer's documentation to deployers on residual identification risk as something supervisors may look at, and EU121 only 'encouraged' generative AI providers to give deployers documentation on detection. The AI Act duties cover high-risk systems only and set no minimum accuracy: the provider chooses and declares the metric and level.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems, often only implied because several articles are passive ('shall be accompanied', 'shall be designed'); deployers, including public bodies [inference], are the recipients. In the EDPS text the supplier of documentation is not named [inference: developer or provider] and the recipient is the controller (an EU institution); in the EP2020 text the knowledge must be available to providers and users; in EU121 the holders are signatories that provide generative AI systems.
themes.binding: Statutory duties on providers in the AI Act ('shall', Arts 9, 13, 14, 15). The passages state no consequence; the 'if not met' field links breach to Art. 16(a) and fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% under Art. 99(4)(a). Recitals use 'should' and are interpretive. EU043 treats provider information as expected but not binding; the EP2020 guideline uses 'must' as an internal rule; the EDPS uses 'should'; EU121 'encourages'.
themes.checks: Trigger: the information accompanies the system when it is supplied, before use; the EDPS expects the controller's accuracy checks to happen 'regularly'. Compared against: the accuracy level and metrics against which the provider tested and validated the system and 'which can be expected', and the known circumstances that affect performance. Metric or threshold: chosen and declared by the provider; no minimum level or threshold is stated. Who: the provider supplies; the deployer and the persons assigned to oversight interpret outputs and check performance (EDPS: the controller). What happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise that include concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers.
the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the high-risk AI system has been tested and validated and which can be expected

The technical and user documentation of the system, including model cards, should enable the controller of the system to carry out appropriate checks and actions regularly to ensure the accuracy principle.
Knowledge and understanding of the inner workings of a solution considered for deployment must be available to both providers and users.

themes.theme: Competence, authority and conditions for human oversight and review
themes.definition: The people, skills, authority, procedures and working conditions that documents require for those assigned to oversee an AI tool or to review its outputs.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires deployers to assign human oversight to 'natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support' (Art. 26(2)); Recital 91 adds 'an adequate level of AI literacy', while Recital 73 frames the same competence as part of the measures a provider identifies, so the texts are not fully consistent on who must secure it. Testing in real-world conditions may only be done through persons who are 'suitably qualified' and have 'the necessary capacity, training and authority' (Art. 60(4)(j)). The Commission's guidelines on prohibited practices (EU043) apply this to law enforcement uses, including remote biometric identification and crime-risk tools: the overseer should understand 'when it underperforms or malfunctions', procedures should define the human role 'in verifying and interpreting the output', staff should be able 'to meaningfully assess the outputs', and, following the EDPB, the workplace should counteract automation bias rather than foster 'uncritical acceptance of the results'. For AI-generated text, the Article 50 guidelines make the human-review exception depend on persons with 'relevant knowledge and professional judgement', who may rely on professional or deontological standards, and EU121 asks signatory deployers to record the human resources allocated to human review before publication. The Commission's internal texts treat this as staff knowledge rather than a formal role: staff 'must be aware' that models can produce 'biased and wrong answers' (EC 2023), and will be helped to 'critically assess outputs' (AIatEC). No passage says how competence is judged, how much time reviewers have, or which cases must reach a human.
themes.holders: Deployers (AI Act Art. 26(2), Recital 91), with Recital 73 pointing to providers' measures; providers or deployers running real-world tests (Art. 60(4)(j)); law enforcement deployers in EU043, where the text is often passive and the deployer is the nearest actor; deployers relying on the Article 50 human-review exception; signatory deployers under EU121; Commission staff, and the AI@EC Network, ISG-AI and HR for the Commission's learning offer.
themes.binding: Statutory for deployers under Art. 26(2) (the 'if not met' field points to Art. 99(4)(e), outside this part) and a condition for real-world testing (if not met, testing may not be conducted). Recitals and EU043 use 'should' (non-binding interpretation). In the Article 50 guidelines qualified human review is a condition: without it the exception does not apply [inference from the coder note]. EU121 is a commitment for signatories with no stated consequence. EC 2023 'must be aware' is internal policy with no stated consequence; AIatEC is a plan ('will').
themes.checks: Trigger: whenever oversight is assigned during use; during real-world testing before placing on the market; before publication for AI-generated text under Article 50. Compared against: not stated; EU043 asks overseers to recognise when the system 'underperforms or malfunctions' and to understand its capabilities and limitations. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: natural persons assigned by the deployer; for remote biometric identification, a human agent who verifies and interprets the output; for Commission staff, every user (coder note: Rule 2 asks for critical assessment of every response). What happens with the result: not stated; no passage says what a reviewer may do on finding an error, or which outputs are routed to a human.

quotes.quote: natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support
Those persons should have clear procedures, training and the necessary competence and authority to meaningfully assess the outputs of the AI system .
one or more natural persons possessing relevant knowledge and professional judgement pertaining to the subject matter under scrutiny

themes.theme: AI literacy duty on providers and deployers
themes.definition: The general duty on providers and deployers to give staff who operate or use AI enough AI literacy, with its restatements and its amendment.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 4 of the AI Act requires providers and deployers to 'take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy' of their staff and others operating or using AI on their behalf, taking account of their knowledge, experience and context; the coder note records that it applies to all AI systems, not only high-risk ones. Recital 20 explains the aim as equipping providers, deployers and affected persons to 'make informed decisions'. The Commission's guidelines restate the duty: EU043 cites it in support of human verification (using 'users' for deployers), and the Article 50 guidelines say the literacy requirements 'also apply' to providers and deployers of chatbots and generative systems. The Digital Omnibus rewrites the duty as 'shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy', dropping 'ensure' and 'a sufficient level' [inference: a weaker obligation], and moves active support to the Commission and Member States (see the next theme). None of the passages says what level is sufficient or links literacy to particular tasks such as checking outputs.
themes.holders: Providers and deployers of AI systems (public bodies are deployers when they use AI [inference]); Recital 20 names no holder.
themes.binding: Statutory duty ('shall') but a best-efforts one ('to their best extent'); the 'if not met' field records that Art. 4 is not among the provisions given a fine ceiling in Art. 99, and no consequence is stated. The Omnibus version stays 'shall' but only to 'support the development' of literacy. The recital and the Commission guidelines are interpretive.

quotes.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf

quotes.location: Art. 1(5), replacing AI Act Art. 4(1); p. 16
quotes.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf
Literacy requirements under Article 4 AI Act also apply to both providers and deployers of AI systems within the scope of Article 50 AI Act.

themes.definition: Literacy and awareness support that EU bodies and Member States offer or are asked to offer, as distinct from the duty on operators themselves.
themes.what_is_set_out: Under the AI Act the Board 'should' and 'may' support the Commission in promoting AI literacy tools and public awareness of the benefits, risks, safeguards, rights and obligations of AI (Recital 20, Art. 66(f)), a supporting rather than a providing role. The Digital Omnibus turns this into a duty: the Commission and the Member States 'shall support and facilitate' providers' and deployers' literacy efforts, 'in particular SMEs', and the Commission is to publish practical examples on the single information platform (coder note). The 2025 JRC report (JRC143539) addresses public administrations' own staff: Member States 'should support their staff to become AI literate', through role-specific training, curated learning resources and peer exchange via the Commission's repository of AI literacy practices, and are encouraged to use EDIHs and the AI skills academy. The Omnibus support is aimed mainly at small firms, while the JRC recommendation calls for an adequate level of AI literacy within public administrations (coder note on its heading).
themes.holders: The European AI Board, supporting the Commission (AI Act); the Commission and Member States (Omnibus Art. 4(2)); Member States, with the Commission's repository, EDIHs and the AI skills academy as instruments (JRC143539).
themes.binding: AI Act: recital 'should' and Board power 'may'. Omnibus: statutory duty on the Commission and Member States to 'support and facilitate', with no stated consequence. JRC143539: recommendation ('should', 'potential measures', 'encouraged').

quotes.location: Art. 1(5), replacing AI Act Art. 4(2); p. 16
quotes.quote: The Commission and the Member States shall support and facilitate the efforts of providers and deployers of AI systems, in particular SMEs, in fulfilling their obligation under paragraph 1 of this Article.
In line with Article 4 of the AI Act, Member States should support their staff to become AI literate.
support the Commission in promoting AI literacy, public awareness and understanding of the benefits, risks, safeguards and rights and obligations in relation to the use of AI systems

themes.theme: Information and technical access along the AI value chain
themes.definition: Information, technical access and help that one supplier in the AI supply chain must or should give another so that the downstream party can build, test and comply.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of general-purpose AI models must 'draw up, keep up-to-date and make available information and documentation' to providers who integrate the model (Art. 53(1)(b); Recital 101), with a minimum set in Annex XII: the technical means for integration and information on the data used for training, testing and validation, including provenance and curation; the coder note adds that Annex XII also covers versions and architecture, and that the duty is subject to intellectual property protection. Where another party becomes the provider of a high-risk system (for example a deployer that substantially modifies it), the initial provider must make available information, technical access and assistance (Art. 25(2); Recital 86), and the Digital Omnibus rewrites this as 'targeted technical access, including for testing and validation', backed by fines under Art. 99(4)(da). Recital 88 asks suppliers of tools, services and components to provide information, capabilities and technical access 'by written agreement'. EU090 adds that transparency about training content 'may also assist' downstream providers to assess the diversity of the data. [inference] A public body that builds a tool on a general-purpose model, or substantially modifies a high-risk system, would be a recipient of these resources; none of the passages names public bodies.
themes.holders: Providers of general-purpose AI models; initial or former providers of high-risk systems; third-party suppliers of AI tools, services and components; the recipients are downstream or new providers.
themes.binding: Art. 53(1)(b) and Art. 25(2) are statutory duties (coder note: Art. 101 fines for general-purpose model providers, outside this part); the Omnibus attaches administrative fines to Art. 25(2)(c). Recitals 86, 88 and 101 use 'should'. EU090 describes a benefit, not a duty.
themes.checks: Trigger: when a model is integrated, or when a party becomes the provider. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the downstream or new provider uses the information and access for its own testing and validation (Omnibus: 'including for testing and validation'). What happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: draw up, keep up-to-date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the general-purpose AI model into their AI systems

quotes.location: Art. 1(12)(a), replacing AI Act Art. 25(2)(c); p.…

should provide by written agreement this provider with the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art
transparency of the general characteristics of the content used for training may also assist providers integrating these models into downstream applications to assess the diversity of the data.

themes.theme: Legal access to data for training, testing and bias detection
themes.definition: Legal permissions and public data infrastructure that give providers access to data for training, validating and testing AI, and for detecting and correcting bias.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act mostly supplies data by granting legal permission rather than datasets. Providers 'may exceptionally process special categories of personal data' where strictly necessary for detecting and correcting bias, under conditions that include having no workable synthetic or anonymised alternative and pseudonymisation (Art. 10(5); Recital 70). In sandboxes, personal data 'lawfully collected for other purposes' may be used to develop, train and test AI built to safeguard a substantial public interest, explicitly including by a public authority, but only 'when all of the following conditions are met' (Art. 59(1); Recital 140, which the coder note says gives no basis under Art. 22(2)(b) GDPR). As infrastructure, European common data spaces 'will be instrumental' for access to high-quality data, competent authorities 'may also support' the provision of such data, and the Commission 'may' work to lower barriers to cross-border data exchange (Recitals 68 and 165). All the passages come from the AI Act itself; no one is obliged to supply data.
themes.holders: Providers, and prospective providers in sandboxes including public authorities; the Commission (common data spaces, cross-border initiatives); relevant competent authorities, including sectoral ones.
themes.binding: Art. 10(5) and Art. 59(1) are statutory permissions with strict conditions; outside those conditions the processing is not allowed. The recitals use 'should', 'will' and 'may'.
themes.checks: Bias detection: trigger not stated (during development); compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: providers; what happens with the result: bias is to be corrected (coder note, Art. 10(2)(f)-(g)). Testing on reused personal data in sandboxes: see the sandbox themes in part 2.

quotes.quote: the providers of such systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons

personal data lawfully collected for other purposes may be processed solely for the purpose of developing, training and testing certain AI systems in the sandbox when all of the following conditions are met

European common data spaces established by the Commission and the facilitation of data sharing between businesses and with government in the public interest will be instrumental to provide trustful, accountable and non-discriminatory access to high-quality data

themes.theme: Templates and inputs for fundamental rights impact assessment
themes.definition: Templates, interim guidance and reusable inputs offered to deployers for the fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) required by Article 27 of the AI Act.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Office 'shall develop a template for a questionnaire, including through an automated tool' so that deployers can meet their FRIA duty 'in a simplified manner' (Art. 27(5); Recital 96), and the Digital Omnibus repeats this, adding (per coder note) that the template should allow cross-references to existing assessments. Deployers 'may, in similar cases, rely on previously conducted' FRIAs or on impact assessments 'carried out by provider' (Art. 27(2)), and Recital 96 tells them to use the provider's instructions for use. The Commission's guidelines on prohibited practices (EU043) offer 'preliminary guidance for deployers in this interim period before the AI Office provides a template', including a description of the technology that refers to the provider's documentation. The template is therefore promised rather than delivered in these passages, and the main inputs come from the provider. [inference] Since the FRIA duty falls largely on public bodies and providers of public services, this template is one of the few resources in the cell aimed at public deployers, although these passages do not say so.
themes.holders: The AI Office (template); the Commission (interim guidance in EU043); providers (instructions for use and their own impact assessments); deployers (users of the template).
themes.binding: Statutory duty on the AI Office to develop the template ('shall'), with no deadline in these passages and no stated consequence; reuse of earlier assessments is a permission ('may'); the interim guidance is non-binding.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated in these passages [inference: before first use, under Art. 27(1)]. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the deployer, using the template and the provider's information. What happens with the result: the template also serves the notification to the market surveillance authority (coder note on Art. 27(3)); nothing further is stated.

quotes.quote: The AI Office shall develop a template for a questionnaire, including through an automated tool, to facilitate deployers in complying with their obligations under this Article in a simplified manner.
is aimed to serve as a preliminary guidance for deployers in this interim period before the AI Office provides a template.
The deployer may, in similar cases, rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or existing impact assessments carried out by provider.
the description of the technology underlying the system to explain its functioning (by referencing the available documentation provided by the provider and its name)

themes.definition: Benchmarks, measurement methods, metrics and validation tools that documents offer, list or call for, to measure how well an AI tool performs.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act does not set benchmarks: the Commission is to 'encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies' with metrology and benchmarking authorities (Art. 15(2); Recital 74), the Board 'may' contribute to common criteria and benchmarks (Art. 66(g)), the scientific panel contributes tools and methods 'for evaluating capabilities of general-purpose AI models' (Art. 68(3)(a)(ii)), and sandboxes 'facilitate the development of tools' for testing and benchmarking accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Art. 58(2)(i)). The 2022 JRC handbook (JRC129100), written while the Act was still a proposal, points to ISO work on guidelines for testing AI systems and calls for collecting 'good and bad practices' to identify validation tools and methods. Only the EDPS risk guidance lists concrete measures: an annex of metrics for language, classification and regression tasks and benchmarks such as ROUGE, BLEU, GLUE, HELM, MMLU, ImageNet, WinoBias and FairFace, offered as 'some benchmarks available at the publishing of this report' and, per coder note, 'not intended to be exhaustive'. No passage sets a threshold, says which metric suits which public task, or deals with the consistency or repeatability of outputs.
themes.holders: The Commission (encourages development); the European AI Board and the scientific panel (contribute); AI regulatory sandboxes; ISO (mentioned); the EDPS (compiles the list; the benchmarks are developed by third parties).
themes.binding: Weak throughout: 'encourage, as appropriate', 'may', 'contributing', 'facilitate'; the JRC text is a recommendation and a footnote mention; the EDPS list is guidance. No consequence is attached.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated. Compared against: benchmarks still to be developed (AI Act) or listed public benchmarks (EDPS). Metric or threshold: metrics are named in the EDPS annex, but no threshold appears anywhere. Who: providers and evaluators [inference]; the EDPS addresses EU institutions. What happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies

themes.definition: Access, staff, facilities and fees that make third-party conformity assessment of high-risk AI possible.
themes.what_is_set_out: When a notified body assesses a high-risk system it 'shall be granted full access to the training, validation, and testing data sets used', including through remote means, and, per coder note, on reasoned request once other means are exhausted, to the training and trained models (Annex VII, points 4.3 and 4.5). Notified bodies must themselves have 'permanent availability of sufficient administrative, technical, legal and scientific personnel' with knowledge of the relevant AI systems and data (Art. 31(11)), and the Commission facilitates, 'to the extent possible', access to testing and experimentation facilities for accredited bodies and laboratories (Recital 147). Fees favour small providers: SME interests 'shall be taken into account' and fees reduced in proportion to size (Art. 62(2)), while the Digital Omnibus makes the provider pay the fees for testing and assessment when it applies to the Commission for third-party assessment, paying notified bodies directly (Art. 75(1e)). These resources serve the assessor's checks before a product reaches the market; none is directed at public deployers.
themes.holders: Notified bodies (receive access; must have staff); providers (grant access; pay fees); the Commission (facilitates access to facilities; receives applications under the Omnibus); whoever sets fees is not named (nearest: notified bodies or Member States [inference]).
themes.binding: Statutory: access 'shall be granted', personnel 'shall have', fees 'shall be levied'. The 'if not met' field links notified-body breaches to Art. 99(4)(f), outside this part. Recital 147 is qualified by 'to the extent possible'.
themes.checks: Trigger: before the system is placed on the market, for systems that require third-party assessment. Compared against: the Regulation's requirements [inference]; not stated in the passages. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: notified bodies (and, under the Omnibus, the Commission for Art. 75(1) systems). What happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

themes.theme: Templates and simplified forms for documentation, quality management and post-market monitoring
themes.definition: Templates, simplified forms and guidance that help providers prepare technical documentation, quality management systems and post-market monitoring plans.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act required the Commission to adopt an implementing act 'establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan' by 2 February 2026 (Art. 72(3)); the Digital Omnibus replaces this with 'guidance, including a template' by 2 September 2027, and its Recital 41 calls it a 'voluntary template' (coder note), so the instrument becomes both softer and later. Small firms receive a 'simplified technical documentation form' that notified bodies must accept (Art. 11(1)), and guidelines on which parts of the quality management system can be met 'in a simplified manner', first for microenterprises (Art. 63(1); Recital 146) and, after the Omnibus, for all SMEs. The quality management system must itself include 'resource management, including security-of-supply related measures' (Art. 17(1)(l)). These are provider-side tools; the passages offer no matching template for a deployer's own monitoring of a tool in use.
themes.holders: The Commission (templates, forms and guidelines; under the Omnibus taking utmost account of the Board's opinion); providers of high-risk systems (resource management in the quality management system); notified bodies (must accept the simplified form, per coder note).
themes.binding: Statutory duties on the Commission ('shall adopt', 'shall establish', 'shall develop'), with deadlines for the monitoring template; no consequence for missing them is stated. Art. 17(1)(l) is a statutory duty on providers (the 'if not met' field points to Art. 99(4)(a) via Art. 16(c)). The Omnibus changes the monitoring template from a binding implementing act to guidance.
themes.checks: Post-market monitoring: trigger: after placing on the market, ongoing [inference from the term]; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: providers; what happens with the result: not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: The Commission shall adopt an implementing act laying down detailed provisions establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan and the list of elements to be included in the plan by 2 February 2026.
